claim: In humans and other mammals, germline mutations are more likely to arise in fathers than in mothers.
source: In humans and other mammals, germline mutations are more likely to arise in fathers than in mothers.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The paternal mutation bias has long been attributed to DNA replication errors in spermatogenesis.
source: Although this sex bias has long been attributed to DNA replication errors in spermatogenesis, recent evidence from humans points to the importance of mutagenic processes that do not depend on cell division, calling into question our understanding of this basic phenomenon.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical understanding in the field.

claim: Recent evidence from humans points to the importance of mutagenic processes that do not depend on cell division.
source: Although this sex bias has long been attributed to DNA replication errors in spermatogenesis, recent evidence from humans points to the importance of mutagenic processes that do not depend on cell division, calling into question our understanding of this basic phenomenon.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies discussed in the introduction.

claim: The ratio of paternal-to-maternal mutations (α) was inferred in 42 species of amniotes.
source: Here, we infer the ratio of paternal-to-maternal mutations, α, in 42 species of amniotes, from putatively neutral substitution rates of sex chromosomes and autosomes.
evidence: This is the main methodological approach of the study.

claim: Fathers consistently contribute more mutations than mothers in all the species examined, including mammals, birds, and reptiles.
source: Despite marked differences in gametogenesis, physiologies and environments across species, fathers consistently contribute more mutations than mothers in all the species examined, including mammals, birds, and reptiles.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: In mammals, α is as high as 4 and correlates with generation times.
source: In mammals, α is as high as 4 and correlates with generation times; in birds and snakes, α appears more stable around 2.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: In birds and snakes, α appears more stable around 2.
source: In mammals, α is as high as 4 and correlates with generation times; in birds and snakes, α appears more stable around 2.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: α may reflect the relative contributions of two or more developmental phases to total germline mutations.
source: Thus, α may reflect the relative contributions of two or more developmental phases to total germline mutations, and is expected to depend on generation time even if mutations do not track cell divisions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: α is expected to depend on generation time even if mutations do not track cell divisions.
source: Thus, α may reflect the relative contributions of two or more developmental phases to total germline mutations, and is expected to depend on generation time even if mutations do not track cell divisions.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: JBS Haldane inferred that the DNM rate at the hemophilia locus is substantially higher in fathers over 70 years ago.
source: This phenomenon was first noted over 70 years ago, when JBS Haldane relied on the population frequency of hemophilia in order to infer that the DNM rate at the disease locus is substantially higher in fathers (Haldane, 1946).
evidence: This is a historical citation to Haldane's work.

claim: Estimates from human pedigrees indicate that genome-wide DNMs occur roughly four times more often on the paternal genome than on the maternal one.
source: Work since then, particularly in molecular evolution, has confirmed a 'male bias' in mutation (henceforth paternal bias) (Makova and Li, 2002; Wolfe and Li, 2003; Li et al., 1996; Presgraves and Yi, 2009; Nachman and Crowell, 2000; Huang et al., 1997; Shimmin et al., 1993b; Chang et al., 1994), with estimates from human pedigrees indicating that, genome-wide, DNMs occur roughly four times more often on the paternal genome than on the maternal one (Kong et al., 2012; Francioli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to pedigree studies.

claim: In humans, oocytes are arrested in meiotic prophase I at birth, with no subsequent DNA replication in the mother's life.
source: In humans as in other mammals, oocytes are arrested in meiotic prophase I at birth, with no subsequent DNA replication in the mother's life, whereas spermatogonia start dividing shortly before puberty and divide continuously throughout the reproductive life of the father (Drost and Lee, 1995; Guo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about known biology supported by citations.

claim: Spermatogonia start dividing shortly before puberty and divide continuously throughout the reproductive life of the father.
source: In humans as in other mammals, oocytes are arrested in meiotic prophase I at birth, with no subsequent DNA replication in the mother's life, whereas spermatogonia start dividing shortly before puberty and divide continuously throughout the reproductive life of the father (Drost and Lee, 1995; Guo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about known biology supported by citations.

claim: The number of DNMs increases with paternal age.
source: The observation that the number of DNMs increases with paternal age has been widely interpreted in this light, as evidence for DNA replication errors being the predominant source of germline mutation (Kong et al., 2012; Francioli et al., 2015; Goldmann et al., 2019; Jónsson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Analyses of large numbers of human pedigrees revealed an effect of maternal age on the number of maternal DNMs, with an additional ∼0.4 mutations accrued per year.
source: First, analyses of large numbers of human pedigrees revealed an effect of maternal age on the number of maternal DNMs (Wong et al., 2016; Goldmann et al., 2016), with an additional ∼0.4 mutations accrued per year.
evidence: This is supported by citations to pedigree studies.

claim: Given the lack of mitotic cell division in oocytes after birth, the maternal age effect indicates that by typical reproductive ages, at least half of maternal DNMs arise from DNA damage.
source: Given the lack of mitotic cell division in oocytes after birth, this observation indicates that by typical reproductive ages, at least half of maternal DNMs arise from DNA damage (Jónsson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the maternal age effect and the biology of oocytes, supported by a citation.

claim: Despite highly variable rates of germ cell division over human ontogenesis, germline mutations appear to accumulate with absolute time in both sexes.
source: Second, despite highly variable rates of germ cell division over human ontogenesis, germline mutations appear to accumulate with absolute time in both sexes, resulting in a ratio of paternal-to-maternal germline mutation, α, of around 3.5 at puberty and very little increase with parental ages (Gao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gao et al., 2019.

claim: The ratio of paternal-to-maternal germline mutation, α, is around 3.5 at puberty in humans and shows very little increase with parental ages.
source: Second, despite highly variable rates of germ cell division over human ontogenesis, germline mutations appear to accumulate with absolute time in both sexes, resulting in a ratio of paternal-to-maternal germline mutation, α, of around 3.5 at puberty and very little increase with parental ages (Gao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gao et al., 2019.

claim: Studies in a dozen other mammals suggest that α ranges from 2 to 4 whether the species reproduces months, years, or decades after birth.
source: Third, studies in a dozen other mammals suggest that α ranges from 2 to 4 whether the species reproduces months, years, or decades after birth (Wu et al., 2020; Wilson Sayres et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2022a), when estimates of germ cell division numbers at time of reproduction would predict a much wider range in α (Drost and Lee, 1995; Lindsay et al., 2019; Harland et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Estimates of germ cell division numbers at time of reproduction would predict a much wider range in α than is observed.
source: Third, studies in a dozen other mammals suggest that α ranges from 2 to 4 whether the species reproduces months, years, or decades after birth (Wu et al., 2020; Wilson Sayres et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2022a), when estimates of germ cell division numbers at time of reproduction would predict a much wider range in α (Drost and Lee, 1995; Lindsay et al., 2019; Harland et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing observed α values with predictions from cell division models, supported by citations.

claim: Most germline mutations arise from the interplay between damage and repair rather than from replication errors.
source: A more parsimonious alternative is that most germline mutations arise from the interplay between damage and repair rather than from replication errors (Seplyarskiy et al., 2021), and that the balance results in more mutations on the paternal than the maternal genome (Gao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors and supported by citations.

claim: 75% of DNMs in humans are due to mutation signatures SBS5/40.
source: Analyses of the mutation spectrum in humans indicate that 75% of DNMs and 80% of mutations in adult seminiferous tubules are due to mutation 'signatures' SBS5/40 (Rahbari et al., 2016; Moore et al., 2021), which are clock-like, uncorrelated with cell division rates in the soma (Alexandrov et al., 2015; Alexandrov et al., 2020), and also predominant in post-mitotic cell types such as neurons (Lodato et al., 2018; Abascal et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mutation spectrum studies.

claim: 80% of mutations in adult seminiferous tubules are due to mutation signatures SBS5/40.
source: Analyses of the mutation spectrum in humans indicate that 75% of DNMs and 80% of mutations in adult seminiferous tubules are due to mutation 'signatures' SBS5/40 (Rahbari et al., 2016; Moore et al., 2021), which are clock-like, uncorrelated with cell division rates in the soma (Alexandrov et al., 2015; Alexandrov et al., 2020), and also predominant in post-mitotic cell types such as neurons (Lodato et al., 2018; Abascal et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mutation spectrum studies.

claim: Mutation signatures SBS5/40 are clock-like and uncorrelated with cell division rates in the soma.
source: Analyses of the mutation spectrum in humans indicate that 75% of DNMs and 80% of mutations in adult seminiferous tubules are due to mutation 'signatures' SBS5/40 (Rahbari et al., 2016; Moore et al., 2021), which are clock-like, uncorrelated with cell division rates in the soma (Alexandrov et al., 2015; Alexandrov et al., 2020), and also predominant in post-mitotic cell types such as neurons (Lodato et al., 2018; Abascal et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mutation signature studies.

claim: Mutation signatures SBS5/40 are predominant in post-mitotic cell types such as neurons.
source: Analyses of the mutation spectrum in humans indicate that 75% of DNMs and 80% of mutations in adult seminiferous tubules are due to mutation 'signatures' SBS5/40 (Rahbari et al., 2016; Moore et al., 2021), which are clock-like, uncorrelated with cell division rates in the soma (Alexandrov et al., 2015; Alexandrov et al., 2020), and also predominant in post-mitotic cell types such as neurons (Lodato et al., 2018; Abascal et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mutation studies in neurons.

claim: Most substitutions in post-pubertal germ cell tumors are attributed to SBS5/40, in both females and males.
source: In addition, most substitutions in post-pubertal germ cell tumors are attributed to SBS5/40, in both females and males (Oliver et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oliver et al., 2022.

claim: Cell division rates do not appear to be a major determinant of mutation rates across somatic tissues.
source: More generally, cell division rates do not appear to be a major determinant of mutation rates across somatic tissues (Blokzijl et al., 2016): notably, post-mitotic neurons accumulate mutations at a similar rate as mitotic somatic cell types that are the product of ongoing cell divisions (Abascal et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on somatic mutation rates.

claim: Post-mitotic neurons accumulate mutations at a similar rate as mitotic somatic cell types that are the product of ongoing cell divisions.
source: More generally, cell division rates do not appear to be a major determinant of mutation rates across somatic tissues (Blokzijl et al., 2016): notably, post-mitotic neurons accumulate mutations at a similar rate as mitotic somatic cell types that are the product of ongoing cell divisions (Abascal et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Abascal et al., 2021.

claim: A decoupling between cell division numbers and mutation burden has been described in colonic crypts across mammals.
source: A decoupling between cell division numbers and mutation burden has also been described in colonic crypts across mammals (Cagan et al., 2022), and in yeast, up to 90% of mutations have been estimated to be non-replicative in origin (Zhou et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cagan et al., 2022.

claim: In yeast, up to 90% of mutations have been estimated to be non-replicative in origin.
source: A decoupling between cell division numbers and mutation burden has also been described in colonic crypts across mammals (Cagan et al., 2022), and in yeast, up to 90% of mutations have been estimated to be non-replicative in origin (Zhou et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2021.

claim: In birds as in mammals, oogenesis is arrested by birth in females, while spermatogenesis is ongoing throughout male reproductive life.
source: As two examples, in birds as in mammals, oogenesis is arrested by birth in females, while spermatogenesis is ongoing throughout male reproductive life (Guraya, 1989; Deviche et al., 2011), but birds have internal testes whereas mammals usually have external testes.
evidence: This is a statement about known biology supported by citations.

claim: Birds have internal testes whereas mammals usually have external testes.
source: As two examples, in birds as in mammals, oogenesis is arrested by birth in females, while spermatogenesis is ongoing throughout male reproductive life (Guraya, 1989; Deviche et al., 2011), but birds have internal testes whereas mammals usually have external testes.
evidence: This is a statement about known anatomy.

claim: Mammals and birds are endotherms, in contrast to ectothermic reptiles such as snakes.
source: In addition, mammals and birds are endotherms, in contrast to ectothermic reptiles such as snakes.
evidence: This is a statement about known physiology.

claim: At the population level, sex chromosomes spend different numbers of generations in each sex.
source: It takes advantage of the fact that at the population level, sex chromosomes spend different numbers of generations in each sex (e.g., the X chromosome spends twice as many generations in females as in males), whereas autosomes spend an equal number in both (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a theoretical principle illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The X chromosome spends twice as many generations in females as in males.
source: It takes advantage of the fact that at the population level, sex chromosomes spend different numbers of generations in each sex (e.g., the X chromosome spends twice as many generations in females as in males), whereas autosomes spend an equal number in both (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a theoretical principle illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Autosomes spend an equal number of generations in both sexes.
source: It takes advantage of the fact that at the population level, sex chromosomes spend different numbers of generations in each sex (e.g., the X chromosome spends twice as many generations in females as in males), whereas autosomes spend an equal number in both (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a theoretical principle illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: If there is a paternal mutation bias, an autosome with greater exposure to the more mutagenic male germline will accumulate more neutral substitutions than the X over evolutionary timescales.
source: Thus, all else being equal, if there is a paternal mutation bias, an autosome with greater exposure to the more mutagenic male germline will accumulate more neutral substitutions than the X over evolutionary timescales (Figure 1A); the inverse will be true for the autosomes compared to the Z chromosome (Miyata et al., 1987).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the Miyata et al. framework, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The inverse relationship will be true for the autosomes compared to the Z chromosome.
source: Thus, all else being equal, if there is a paternal mutation bias, an autosome with greater exposure to the more mutagenic male germline will accumulate more neutral substitutions than the X over evolutionary timescales (Figure 1A); the inverse will be true for the autosomes compared to the Z chromosome (Miyata et al., 1987).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the Miyata et al. framework.

claim: The filtering procedure resulted in three whole genome alignments including 20 mammals, 17 birds, and 5 snake species.
source: This stringent filtering procedure resulted in three whole genome alignments including 20 mammals, 17 birds, and 5 snake species, respectively (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes the final dataset used in the study.

claim: The point estimates for species with the largest amount of available DNM data (e.g., humans, mice, and cattle) are in very close agreement.
source: Notably, and reassuringly, the point estimates for species with the largest amount of available DNM data (e.g., humans, mice, and cattle) are in very close agreement.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing α_evo and α_dnm values.

claim: A paternal bias in mutation is seen across amniotes, with a range of 1–4 in the species considered.
source: A paternal bias in mutation is seen across amniotes, with a range of 1–4 in the species considered (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding shown in Figure 2.

claim: The paternal bias in mutation is not a feature of long-lived humans or of mammals, but is instead ubiquitous across species that vary markedly in their gametogenesis, physiology, and life history.
source: These results therefore establish that the paternal bias in mutation is not a feature of long-lived humans or of mammals, but is instead ubiquitous across species that vary markedly in their gametogenesis, physiology, and life history.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data from 42 species across amniotes.

claim: In mammals, variation in α has long been known to be associated with generation times.
source: In mammals, variation in α has long been known to be associated with generation times, and has been consistently interpreted as resulting from greater numbers of replication errors in species with longer-lived fathers (e.g., Wilson Sayres et al., 2011; Chang et al., 1994; Li et al., 1996; Li et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings in the literature.

claim: In eutherian mammals, embryo development is likely independent of sex until primordial germ cell (PGC) specification and subsequent development of the gonads.
source: In eutherian mammals, embryo development is likely independent of sex until primordial germ cell (PGC) specification and subsequent development of the gonads (Lin and Capel, 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about known developmental biology supported by a citation.

claim: Human fathers that recently reached puberty contribute over three times more mutations than similarly aged mothers.
source: Indeed, human fathers that recently reached puberty contribute over three times more mutations than similarly aged mothers (Gao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gao et al., 2019.

claim: The magnitude of paternal bias for mutations that occurred long after sexual differentiation of the PGCs appears to be similar in mice, cattle, and humans, at approximately 4:1.
source: Intriguingly, the magnitude of paternal bias for mutations that occurred long after sexual differentiation of the PGCs appears to be similar in mice, cattle, and humans, at approximately 4:1 (Lindsay et al., 2019; Harland et al., 2017; Sasani et al., 2019; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from pedigree studies shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The increased α seen in long-lived mammals may simply reflect a reduction in the fraction of early embryonic mutations relative to total number of mutations per generation.
source: In any case, this phenomenological model clarifies that the increased α seen in long-lived mammals may simply reflect a reduction in the fraction of early embryonic mutations relative to total number of mutations per generation – consistent with the higher proportion of Early mutations in mice and cattle compared to humans (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model results, supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: The model can explain the only modest increase in α with parental ages observed in humans.
source: This model can also explain the only modest increase in α with parental ages observed in humans (Gao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a claim about the explanatory power of the model, with a citation.

claim: Avian sexual phenotype is directly determined by the sex chromosome content of individual cells.
source: Unlike mammals, avian sexual phenotype is directly determined by the sex chromosome content of individual cells (Zhao et al., 2010; Ioannidis et al., 2021) and PGCs are determined by inheritance of maternally derived gene products (Extavour and Akam, 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about known avian biology supported by citations.

claim: PGCs in birds are determined by inheritance of maternally derived gene products.
source: Unlike mammals, avian sexual phenotype is directly determined by the sex chromosome content of individual cells (Zhao et al., 2010; Ioannidis et al., 2021) and PGCs are determined by inheritance of maternally derived gene products (Extavour and Akam, 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about known avian biology supported by a citation.

claim: Sex differences in the cellular phenotypes of PGCs prior to gonad development have been reported in birds.
source: Given these features, it seems plausible that sex differences in mutation rates appear earlier in ontogenesis in birds than in mammals, consistent with reported sex differences in the cellular phenotypes of PGCs prior to gonad development (Soler et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Soler et al., 2021.

claim: The proximate causes of the paternal bias are likely sex differences in endogenous sources of DNA damage or in repair mechanisms.
source: Given that the paternal bias varies little across species exposed to disparate physical environments, and presumably distinct exogenous mutagens, the proximate causes of the paternal bias are likely sex differences in endogenous sources of DNA damage or in repair mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that α is relatively stable across diverse environments.

claim: The effects of reactive oxygen species, a major source of DNA damage, may be greater in male germ cells than in oocytes.
source: For instance, the effects of reactive oxygen species, a major source of DNA damage, may be greater in male germ cells than in oocytes (Smith et al., 2013; Rodríguez-Nuevo et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: The evolutionary cause of the paternal bias could be related to the different evolutionary pressures acting on each sex of anisogamous species, for example due to greater competition among sperm than among oocytes.
source: In turn, the evolutionary cause of the paternal bias could be related to the different evolutionary pressures acting on each sex of anisogamous species, for example due to greater competition among sperm than among oocytes.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the evolutionary cause.

claim: The balance of damage and repair results in an approximately fourfold higher mutation rate in spermatogonia compared to oocytes across mammalian species.
source: The balance of damage and repair results in an approximately fourfold higher mutation rate in spermatogonia compared to oocytes across mammalian species (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Comparing yearly mutation rates in colonic crypts to estimates for spermatogonia, the ratio of crypt-to-sperm mutation rates appears relatively stable across four mammalian species.
source: Similarly, comparing yearly mutation rates in colonic crypts (Cagan et al., 2022) to estimates for spermatogonia, the ratio of crypt-to-sperm mutation rates appears relatively stable across four mammalian species (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The relative mutagenicity of different cell types may be conserved across mammals.
source: This observation suggests that, beyond spermatogonia and oocytes, the relative mutagenicity of different cell types may be conserved across mammals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the stability of mutation rate ratios across cell types.

claim: Mutation rates in different cell types could be coupled over time either because of natural selection to maintain specific rates in each cell type or because changes to the repair machinery in some cell types have pleiotropic consequences on mutation rates in others.
source: Mutation rates in different cell types could be coupled over time either because of natural selection to maintain specific rates in each cell type or because changes to the repair machinery in some cell types (potentially, germ cells) have pleiotropic consequences on mutation rates in others.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanisms maintaining relative mutation rates.

claim: The observations point to a role of natural selection in maintaining the relative rates at which mutations accumulate in different cell types over long evolutionary timescales.
source: Regardless, our observations point to a role of natural selection in maintaining the relative rates at which mutations accumulate in different cell types over long evolutionary timescales.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the conservation of relative mutation rates across species.
